newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate debates disputed chemical weapons pact.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate debates disputed chemical weapons pact.

text.p: The Senate opened debate on Wednesday on U.S. approval of a global treaty outlawing chemical weapons as its supporters gained a powerful ally -- Bob Dole, last year's Republican presidential candidate.

Dole's surprise appearance at a White House rally for the Chemical Weapons Convention was a major coup for President Bill Clinton. He has put his foreign policy credibility on the line in an all-out lobbying campaign for the treaty.

Treaty supporters said Dole's endorsement boosted prospects that it will get the required two-thirds majority when the Senate votes on Thursday on whether to consent to its ratification by the United States.
It was Dole who, in the midst of the presidential campaign last September, wrote a letter to Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott raising questions about the treaty.

Fearing this would plunge the pact into election-year politics and doom it to defeat, the administration asked that it be pulled from the Senate floor. Dole said on Wednesday that 28 clarifications agreed to by the administration took care of his earlier objections.
"If I were present in the Senate (where he was former Republican leader), I would vote for the CWC because of the many improvements that have been agreed to," Dole said.

In fact, two issues Dole raised last september are still in dispute. Amendments upgrading standards of verifiability against cheating and requiring global membership in the treaty are expected to be struck out by treaty supporters
The 1993 convention, already ratified by more than 70 countries, bans the development, production, stockpiling, transfer and use of chemical weapons.
It goes into effect next Tuesday, with or without the United States. Unless it ratifies the treaty before then, Washington would have no role in implementing it.

Just before the Senate opened two days of debate, Lott, the majority leader and a key player in influencing uncommitted Republicans, said he was waiting to see "the final product" before making up his mind. He was careful not to foreclose the possibility that he would vote for the treaty.

Before the final vote, the Senate will vote on whether to strip out so-called "killer" amendments to the ratification resolution that will decide if in fact the United States can participate in the treaty.
Lott zeroed in on a treaty provision that appears to have become the crucial factor in prospects for ratification.

This is Article 11 under which parties to the treaty "undertake to facilitate, and have the right to participate in, the fullest possible exchange of chemicals, equipment and scientific and technical information" allowed by the treaty.

The article also requires parties not to restrict trade development and promotion of scientific knowledge of chemistry for peaceful purposes and to make their own national regulations consistent with the treaty.

The ratification resolution that emerged from the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, headed by treaty archfoe Jesse Helms, would make U.S. ratification conditional on elimination of these clauses from the treaty and total elimination of Article 10, calling for exchange of chemical arms defence technology.
Helms argues that what he calls the "poisons for peace" provision would enable so-called rogue states to obtain chemical weapons technology.

Of his vote, Lott said: "I will wait to see what we're able to work out with the administration on concerns and how we're addressing Articles 10 and 11 of the convention, and how the votes go tomorrow before making a final decision."

Helms, a North Carolina Republican, opened the Senate debate declaring that the treaty "is worse than nothing" because it would give the American people a false sense of security and would pave the way for technology to go to "rogue states" seeking to build poison gas arsenals.
